strengths: First work to establish logarithmic regret (and linear 1/epsilon sample complexity) for KL-regularized two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games under bandit feedback and linear function approximation.

The core technical idea of using best-response sampling to exploit the closed-form Gibbs structure of regularized best responses, paired with the novel 'super-optimistic' bonus design to control squared Bellman errors, is elegant and original.

The paper carefully resolves a major technical hurdle unique to regularized games: unlike single-agent MDPs where value functions remain strictly bounded in [0, H], regularized games have positive KL terms that can cause values to blow up; the authors cleanly bound the equilibrium values and design appropriate projection operators.
The manuscript is well-structured, clear, and provides detailed, rigorous proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The horizon dependence in the Markov game bound is relatively steep (H^7 in the logarithmic bound and H^3 in the root-T bound), largely due to the O(H^2) projection ceiling required for super-optimism.
The study is purely theoretical and does not provide numerical simulations or toy experiments to demonstrate the empirical behavior and practicality of the super-optimistic bonus mechanism.

Computational considerations could be clarified: Algorithm 2 requires solving stage-wise regularized matrix games and evaluating value functions at next states across the dataset; while the authors mention linear convergence via extragradient methods, a discussion on overall computational complexity would strengthen the presentation.

strengths: First logarithmic regret guarantee for KL-regularized competitive games: The paper successfully closes an open theoretical problem by establishing that KL regularization enables an O(beta^{-1} poly(d, H) log^2 T) regret bound in two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games under bandit feedback, improving upon the standard O(sqrt{T}) regret.

Simultaneous regularization-dependent and independent bounds: The proposed algorithms (OMG and SOMG) attain min{O~(sqrt{T}), O~(beta^{-1} log^2 T)} regret, ensuring robust performance that recovers standard minimax rates when beta -> 0 or for smaller T, without blowing up when regularization is weak.

Novel and insightful algorithmic mechanisms: The paper introduces two clever ideas to handle the technical hurdles of game-theoretic settings: (1) using best-response sampling against the opponent's fixed stage policy to restore closed-form Gibbs policy representations and cancel opponent KL terms in exploitability differences; and (2) designing 'superoptimistic bonuses' and quadratic projection ceilings (3(H - h + 1)^2) to guarantee the superoptimistic gap condition 2(Q^+ - \bar{Q}) >= |Q^+ - Q^\mu|, preventing error propagation across game stages.

Rigorous, detailed, and clear presentation: The paper provides clear structural overviews (Section 4) explaining the core mechanisms and proof flow before providing comprehensive and mathematically rigorous proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: High polynomial horizon and dimension dependence: In the Markov game setting, the regularization-dependent bound scales as O(beta^{-1} d^3 H^7 log^2(dT/delta)). While the authors briefly comment on potential improvements via Bernstein-type concentration bounds in a footnote, an H^7 dependence remains relatively loose.

Lack of empirical evaluation: The submission is purely theoretical. While standard for foundational learning theory contributions, inclusion of even simple synthetic simulations illustrating the empirical regret transition from O(sqrt{T}) to O(log^2 T) as beta varies would provide valuable practical intuition.

Computational considerations: While the stage-wise regularized matrix game can be solved with linear convergence via extragradient methods, the full computational complexity per episode (including solving nested stage matrix games and computing superoptimistic bonuses across continuous/large state spaces) could be discussed more explicitly.

Minor editorial errata: A few minor typos exist throughout the text (e.g., 'uses a the same' on page 9, 'Explotaibility' in equation (32), 'E_3 \cap E_3' instead of 'E_2 \cap E_3' right before equation (59), and 'to \tilde{\nu}_t at t' instead of '\nu_t' on page 31).

strengths: First logarithmic regret guarantee for KL-regularized competitive games: The paper provides the first theoretical result establishing logarithmic regret (and corresponding $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$ sample complexity) in both two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games under bandit feedback.

Clever decoupling via best-response sampling: While Nash equilibria in regularized games lack closed-form Gibbs expressions, the authors observe that best responses to a fixed opponent strategy retain closed-form Gibbs representations. This enables decomposing exploitability into single-agent-like best response regret terms.

Novel super-optimistic bonus and projection design: To handle the fact that KL regularizers can induce large positive value magnitudes and to ensure the requisite variance domination relation ($2(Q^+ - \bar{Q}) \ge |Q^+ - Q^\mu|$) across Bellman backups, the authors formulate a super-optimistic bonus ($b_h + 2b_h^{\text{mse}}$) paired with an expanded clipping ceiling ($3(H-h+1)^2$).

Dual bounds: The algorithms (OMG and SOMG) establish both a regularization-dependent logarithmic bound $\tilde{O}(\beta^{-1} \log^2 T)$ and a regularization-independent rate $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, ensuring robust performance as $\beta \to 0$.
Rigorous and comprehensive theoretical appendix: The mathematical arguments, covering numbers, concentration bounds, and potential lemmas are worked out in detail.
weaknesses: Steep horizon dependence in Markov games: The regularization-dependent regret bound scales with $H^7$ (and sample complexity with $H^7 / \epsilon$), which is relatively loose. While the authors note in Footnote 4 that Bernstein-type bonuses might shave off some factors, tightening the horizon dependence remains an unaddressed challenge.

Lack of empirical verification: The paper is purely theoretical. Even a minimal synthetic simulation (e.g., verifying the regret transition between $O(\sqrt{T})$ and $O(\log^2 T)$ as $\beta$ varies on matrix games or small gridworlds) would have provided valuable corroboration of the theoretical rates.

Strong reliance on single-agent proof templates: Key parts of the regret decomposition and curvature analysis heavily build upon recent single-agent regularized bandit/RL techniques (e.g., Zhao et al., 2025b). While the game-theoretic adaptation via best responses and superoptimism is nontrivial, the conceptual leap from single-agent regularized RL is somewhat incremental.

strengths: First logarithmic regret guarantee for regularized games: The paper establishes the first $O(\log^2(T)/\beta)$ regret bounds and corresponding $O(1/\epsilon)$ sample complexity bounds for both two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games under bandit feedback with linear function approximation.

Technically novel superoptimistic bonus mechanism: Unlike single-agent KL-regularized RL, the Nash equilibrium policies in Markov games do not admit closed-form Gibbs expressions and the value functions can become unbounded due to positive KL terms. The authors resolve these fundamental hurdles by sampling best-response pairs and introducing 'superoptimistic' bonus padding ($b^{\text{sup}} = b + 2b^{\text{mse}}$) alongside elevated projection ceilings ($3(H-h+1)^2$), which guarantees the crucial superoptimistic gap condition holds inductively.

Rigorous covering number analysis: Bounding the metric entropy of the induced value function class in the Markov game setting is technically demanding because it involves best-responding to the opponent's equilibrium policy under a perturbed game. The authors derive new perturbation stability bounds (Lemma C.13) for KL-regularized matrix games to obtain sharp covering number estimates.

Dual bounds: The proposed algorithms (OMG and SOMG) attain both the $\beta$-dependent logarithmic regret bound and the standard $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regularization-independent regret bound simultaneously, avoiding performance degradation when $\beta$ is very small.

Strong motivation and clear exposition: The problem is well-grounded in modern RLHF and multi-agent alignment for large language models, and Section 4 provides an intuitive, high-level walkthrough of the technical mechanisms before diving into the extensive appendix proofs.
weaknesses: High polynomial dependence on horizon $H$: The Markov game regret bound scales as $H^7$ in the logarithmic term (and $H^3$ in the $\sqrt{T}$ term). While footnote 4 mentions that Bernstein-style bonuses might reduce this factor, the current dependence is relatively pessimistic.

Computational tractability in continuous state spaces: While the paper notes that the regularized matrix game subproblems can be solved efficiently via extragradient methods, Algorithm 2 is formulated as a value iteration scheme that implicitly assumes either small/tabular state spaces or an efficient sampling oracle for state-wise matrix game solves during execution.

Lack of empirical evaluation: The paper is purely theoretical. Even a synthetic or stylized numerical simulation demonstrating that OMG/SOMG outperforms standard unregularized UCB / $\sqrt{T}$ baselines in sample efficiency would strengthen the empirical grounding.

strengths: First logarithmic regret guarantee in KL-regularized competitive games: The paper provides the first regret bounds scaling logarithmically with the horizon $T$ (specifically $\widetilde{O}(\beta^{-1} d^2 \log^2 T)$ for matrix games and $\widetilde{O}(\beta^{-1} d^3 H^7 \log^2 T)$ for Markov games) under bandit feedback, translating to an $\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$ sample complexity to find an $\epsilon$-Nash Equilibrium.

Clever technical framework overcoming game-theoretic challenges: Unlike single-agent RL where optimal policies have closed-form Gibbs representations, Nash equilibria in games do not admit closed forms. The authors cleverly overcome this by employing best-response sampling (since best responses to fixed strategies do have closed forms) and decomposing the dual gap accordingly.

Novel superoptimistic bonus mechanism: To handle the potentially unbounded values induced by positive KL regularization terms in two-player zero-sum Markov games and ensure propagation of the variance-like gap condition across steps, the paper introduces a well-motivated superoptimistic bonus and tailored projection operators.

Comprehensive theoretical development: The paper is mathematically thorough, providing complete proofs, careful covering number bounds using payoff perturbation stability (Lemma C.13), and natural reductions to single-agent bandits and RL matching state-of-the-art results.
weaknesses: High polynomial dependence on horizon $H$: The Markov game logarithmic regret scales with $H^7$ (and sample complexity with $H^7 / \epsilon$). While the authors note in a footnote that Bernstein-style variance-aware bonuses could improve this, the current dependence is somewhat loose.

Absence of numerical simulations: Although this is primarily a theoretical paper, even a simple synthetic experiment on a small matrix or Markov game comparing OMG/SOMG against standard unregularized UCB / $\sqrt{T}$ baselines would nicely validate the practical effect of the $\log^2 T$ vs $\sqrt{T}$ scaling.

Computational considerations in large state spaces: While each stage-game regularized NE computation converges linearly via extragradient methods, executing Algorithm 2 in continuous or large state spaces requires evaluating policies and best responses across states, which could be computationally demanding without additional approximation details.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely theoretical question: while single-agent RL with reverse-KL regularization has recently been shown to achieve logarithmic regret, existing game-theoretic analyses under KL regularization were limited to O(sqrt(T)) regret. This paper successfully closes that gap.

The technical design cleverly navigates several unique hurdles in game-theoretic settings: (1) using best-response sampling to bypass the lack of closed-form Nash equilibrium policies, (2) introducing super-optimistic bonuses and adjusted projection operators to manage potentially unbounded value functions from opponent KL terms, and (3) establishing stability of regularized NE under payoff perturbations to bound covering numbers.
Provides the first logarithmic regret bounds and O(1/epsilon) sample complexity guarantees for KL-regularized zero-sum matrix games and linear Markov games under bandit feedback.
The theoretical development is mathematically rigorous, thorough, and well-organized, with detailed proofs spanning across the matrix game and Markov game cases.
weaknesses: The polynomial dependence on the horizon H in the Markov game regret bound is relatively steep (scaling as H^7). While the authors note in Footnote 4 that Bernstein-type bonuses could potentially shave off factors, the current bound remains loose in H.
The work is purely theoretical with no numerical experiments or toy simulations to validate the empirical scaling of regret with respect to T and beta.
Computing the regularized Nash equilibrium at every step/state within Algorithm 2 can be computationally demanding in practical or continuous-state scenarios.

Minor presentation polish is needed: there are slight typographical redundancies (e.g., Algorithm 1 line 1 lists 'Reg. parameter beta, regularization') and small inconsistencies in how logarithmic factors are written between the main paper and Appendix C.
